newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai bourse has a long way to catch Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai bourse has a long way to catch Hong Kong.

text.p: The Shanghai stock exchange is looking at a long hard road to catch its Hong Kong counterpart after China takes over the colony, but could match it in size and maturity within a decade, analysts said on Monday.
Shanghai's bourse is young -- created only seven years ago -- and has a market capitalisation only one-fifth the size of Hong Kong's.
But it is one of the fastest-growing exchanges in the world and turnover can match that of Hong Kong on given days.

Beijing's securities authorities have reined in the speculative exuberance of China's markets in recent weeks, bringing prices down sharply. But analysts said that in the long run, the clampdown would help the markets to mature.
"In 10 years, you could see the Shanghai stock market rivalling Hong Kong in size and in maturity," said Hoare Govett Asia's Bruce Richardson in Shanghai.

"We have big scandals, stock price manipulation and a totally uneducated retail investor base, but my sense is that some investors are learning how to invest in an informed manner rather than playing the odds," he added.
Chinese analysts and officials also see the development of Shanghai's stock market as a long-term task, but with the prospect of catching up with Hong Kong a real possibility.

"For a period after Hong Kong's return to China, the Shanghai stock exchange will continue to attract domestic funds while Hong Kong focuses more on international liquidity," an exchange official said privately.

"But the exchange is developing much more quickly than its Hong Kong counterpart and its competition with Hong Kong and other world-class bourses is not completely out of the question after the year 2000," he said.
The total market capitalisation of the Shanghai bourse is now around 840 billion yuan ($101.2 billion), while that of the Hong Kong stock exchange is around HK$3.6 trillion ($461.5 billion).
Daily turnover in Shanghai is now around nine billion yuan, compared with 9.1 billion yuan for the whole of 1991, the first year of the exchange's operations.
Shanghai hosts 380 listed firms against more than 600 in Hong Kong, but is adding companies at a furious rate -- more than 50 so far this year.
Hong Kong returns to China on July 1 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
The bulk of the firms in Shanghai have domestic currency A share listings, which are off-limits to foreign investors, while only 44 have listed foreign currency B shares.
"We anticipate the Shanghai market will expand rapidly in the next decade," said a China stock analyst with a major foreign brokerage in Hong Kong.
"The central government is grooming Shanghai as a future international financial centre, and they want to speed up the pace of market capitalisation expansion," she added.
The weak international element to the Shanghai market is currently its main problem, the analyst said.
"The crucial factor determining the future prospects of the Shanghai exchange is the accessibility of foreign investors to the domestic stock market," she said.

"For Shanghai to evolve into a genuine international stock exchange, foreign investors have to be in the market. The merger of the A and B shares should be realised within five years, which will make Shanghai much more attractive," the analyst added.
